cases.message: Why did my score drop from 611 to 588 this month?

routing.reason: The member asks why their score dropped, which is a score-changes question, and utilization is a common cause of a drop, so it is also relevant.

cases.reply:
Your score (VantageScore 3.0) went from 611 on September 15 to 588 now. Several things in your profile likely explain it, starting with the biggest.

**The late payment.** Your Retail store card was reported 30 days late on September 28. The payment was due August 25. A new 30-day late payment is one of the largest things that can move a score, and it's the most likely main cause.

**Higher utilization.** Your card balances were reported at $1,410 of $3,000 in limits on October 5, which is 47%. That was up from $900 (30%) the month before. Utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) is a major factor, and a jump like this can pull a score down too. Your Retail store card is at $900 of $1,500, which is 60% on that card alone, so it's a good place to focus.

**A hard inquiry.** You have one hard inquiry from your April personal loan application. It's been on your report for a while, so it's probably a smaller factor now.

Scores can also differ a little between updates because each lender reports on its own schedule. A score drop like this doesn't mean the account is closed or your history is erased.

**What can help from here:** Paying the Retail store card down before its statement closing date lowers the balance reported to the bureaus. Under most current models, high utilization stops weighing as much once a lower balance is reported, usually after the next statement. The late payment will stay on your report for its full reporting period, so keeping every payment on time from here matters most.

Next step: Pay down the Retail store card balance before its next statement closes, and check your statement date in your card account.

cases.message: I've never missed a payment, so why did my score go down 13 points?

routing.reason: The member asks why their score dropped 13 points despite never missing a payment, which is a score-change question that often traces to a higher reported utilization, so score-changes and utilization are the relevant skills.

cases.reply:
Your payment history is a strength, and it isn't the cause of this drop. Your profile shows no late payments and no negative items. The most likely reason is your credit card balances.

Your overall utilization (the share of your credit card limits you're using) rose to 85% ($2,550 of $3,000). It was 70% the month before. That change was reported on October 5. Most of the increase came from a car repair charged to your Rewards card on September 20. That card is now at 95% of its $2,000 limit. Your bank card is at 65% of $1,000.

Utilization is a large part of your score, and it is separate from payment history. Paying on time protects that part of your score, but it doesn't offset high balances. Your score is also now 655 on VantageScore 3.0. Your previous score of 668 was from September 15, before the higher balance was reported.

Two things to keep in mind:

- Lenders report balances on their own schedule, usually once a month near the statement date. A lower balance may not show up in your score until the next report.
- I can't tell you how many points you'll gain back or when. That depends on your full credit report and the model a lender uses.

Lowering your balances will help most, especially on the Rewards card. Paying it down before its statement closing date means a lower balance gets reported.

Next step: Check your Rewards card's statement closing date and make a payment that brings its balance down before that date.

cases.message: A lender told me I don't have a FICO score. How long until I get one?

cases.message: I've paid rent on time for over two years. Why does Rent Reporting only show 4 months?

routing.reason: The member asks why Rent Reporting shows only 4 months despite two years of on-time rent, which falls under rent-reporting's coverage of adding up to 12 months of past rent and how reported rent is counted.

cases.reply:
Rent Reporting only counts months since you enrolled. Your profile shows you signed up on June 1, 2026, and 4 on-time months have been reported since then (June through September). Your lease started in September 2024, but the app doesn't go back to those earlier months unless you choose to add them.

Here's how it works:

- **Past rent is optional.** You can add up to 12 months of past rent for a one-time $25 fee. Your profile shows you chose not to add it when you enrolled.
- **The limit is 12 months.** Even with past rent added, the app can't cover your full two years.
- **Only on-time payments count.** Your October rent ($1,400) was paid on time, but it isn't reported yet. Reporting also depends on the payment being verified through your linked bank account.
- **Where it shows up.** Rent is reported to TransUnion and Experian. It is not reported to Equifax.
- **Whether it helps your score varies.** Some scoring models count rent and some don't. Your mortgage lender will choose which score it uses, so ask them about it when you apply in 2027.

Next step: Check your linked bank account in the app to confirm your October rent payment went through, and tell human support (Help > Chat with support) if it doesn't show as verified within the next billing cycle.

cases.message: When will the phone company collection come off my credit report?

routing.reason: The member asks when a phone company collection will fall off their report, which is a collections question about how long collection accounts stay.

cases.reply:
Based on your profile, the phone company collection should come off your credit report around March 2029.

The collection's original delinquency date is March 14, 2022. Collections can stay on credit reports for up to 7 years from that first missed-payment date. Paying the debt or having it sold to another collector does not restart that clock. So the 7 years run from March 2022, not from when it was reported in September 2022 or when you pay.

Paying the $1,200 would not remove it early. It would show as paid, and it would still stay until the 7-year date. Paid collections are also ignored by some newer scoring models, such as VantageScore 3.0, which your profile uses. Whether it's worth paying is your call, and you may want to think about it alongside your other debts.

Next step: Look at the collection agency's letter from September 22 and check that the $1,200 amount and the phone company's name match your records.

cases.reply:
Right now, the cost is $0. Your profile shows no fees charged, and no settlement has been agreed yet. You're still negotiating with the bank card creditor.

The fee is 20% of the amount saved. The amount saved is your balance minus the settlement amount. It is charged only after a settlement is agreed and you make at least one payment under it. There are no upfront fees.

Here's an example using your $2,800 balance. These numbers are hypothetical, not a prediction:

- Settled for $1,680: $1,120 saved, $224 fee, $1,904 total paid.

Two other points:
- Settlement isn't guaranteed, and the creditor doesn't have to agree.
- Negotiating doesn't stop collection calls, lawsuits, or interest.

You can also negotiate with the creditor yourself for free, or talk with a nonprofit credit counselor.

Next step: Ask the Debt Settlement team for the fee and payment terms in writing before you agree to any settlement or make a payment.

cases.message: How long will the late payment from 2024 stay on my credit report?

routing.reason: The member asks how long a 2024 late payment stays on the report, which is a payment-history question about reporting duration and fading impact.

cases.reply:
Your profile shows one late payment: your bank credit card was reported 30 days late, with the original late date of November 12, 2024 (reported December 16, 2024).

Under federal rules, a late payment like this can stay on your credit reports for up to 7 years from the original late date. That means it could stay until about November 2031. Closing the account would not remove it sooner. Its effect on your score usually shrinks as it ages and as on-time payments build up.

Some useful points:
- Paying the account on time going forward helps more over time than anything else.
- If you think the late mark is wrong, you can dispute it with the credit bureau and with the bank. You'd need documents, such as statements showing you paid on time.
- If you think it's accurate, you can ask the bank for a goodwill letter, which asks them to remove it as a courtesy. They don't have to agree, and I can't promise they will.

Next step: Check your bank card's payment history for November 2024 to confirm the details match your own records.

cases.message: When will my Credit Builder payments start showing on my credit report? And should I also get a secured card?

cases.reply:
**When your payments show up**

Each Credit Builder payment is reported to Equifax, Experian and TransUnion once a month, a few days after it posts. Your profile shows 4 on-time payments so far, the most recent on October 1, 2026. That payment should appear within the next few days if it hasn't already. I can't see what the bureaus have on file, so check your report there to confirm.

**Whether to add a secured card**

A secured card is a credit card backed by a deposit you pay up front. Here is what it involves:

- **Deposit:** $50 to $2,000. Your credit limit equals the deposit. The deposit is refundable, but it's money you can't spend while the card is open.
- **Applying:** no hard inquiry (a check that can slightly lower a score), and no annual fee.
- **Interest:** a variable APR (interest rate) of 27.99%, charged only on balances you carry from month to month.
- **Upgrade:** after 8 consecutive on-time payments, the account is reviewed for an upgrade to an unsecured card, and your deposit is returned if upgraded.

A card would add a revolving account, which your Credit Builder plan isn't. Revolving credit is tracked by utilization (how much of your limit you're using). Your profile shows no card and no utilization yet. Keeping balances low and paying in full each month is what matters if you get one. I can't say how a card would change your score.

Whether it makes sense depends on whether you can pay the balance in full every month. If you're not sure, ask human support to walk through it.

Next step: Check your credit report at the three bureaus in a few days to confirm your October 1 payment has been reported.

cases.message:
Few questions:
1. Would rent reporting actually do anything for my score?
2. If I'm ever short on rent and it ends up with a collection agency, would paying it off later make it go away?
3. Once my secured card shows up, how long until I get my $300 deposit back?

routing.reason: Three questions: whether rent reporting affects score (rent-reporting), whether paying a rent collection later removes it (collections), and when the secured card deposit is returned (secured-card).

cases.reply:
**1. Would rent reporting do anything for my score?**

It might, but it depends on two things. Rent Reporting sends on-time rent to TransUnion and Experian only, not Equifax. It also only helps if the score model counts rent. FICO 8 ignores rent, while some newer models (FICO 9, FICO 10, VantageScore 3.0 and 4.0) can count it. Your profile shows your score as VantageScore 3.0, which can count rent, but it doesn't say which bureau or model each lender uses. Lenders choose their own, so the effect varies. Rent Reporting costs $4 per month. You don't have it set up on your profile now.

**2. If I miss rent and it goes to collections, would paying it later make it go away?**

Not necessarily. Paying a non-medical collection doesn't remove it from your report. It shows as paid. A collection can stay up to 7 years from the first missed payment, and paying doesn't restart that clock. Some newer score models ignore paid collections, but FICO 8 still counts them unless the original balance was under $100. Also, the app doesn't report late or missed rent. The collection agency's report is what can show up, not the app.

**3. Once my secured card arrives, how long until I get my $300 deposit back?**

The app doesn't give a set timeline for returning the deposit. Here's what I can confirm: the deposit is refundable, and it can be returned if your card is upgraded to an unsecured card. That review happens after 8 consecutive on-time payments. Your profile shows 0 on-time payments so far, because the card hasn't been activated yet. For a timeline on a deposit refund, ask human support.

Next step: Once the card arrives, activate it in the app before you use it, and make your first payment on time.

Your profile shows your next Credit Builder payment is due November 1, 2026. Each payment is reported to Equifax, Experian and TransUnion once a month, a few days after it posts. cases.reply:
Three questions, so here they are in order.

**1. Does Credit Builder count toward utilization?**
No. Utilization is about revolving accounts like credit cards, where you carry a balance against a limit. Credit Builder is an installment plan with fixed payments and an end date, so it isn't part of utilization. Your profile shows $0 in revolving balances and $0 in revolving limits, so there's no utilization figure to report yet. Credit Builder still adds to your credit mix, and its on-time payments are reported to all three bureaus.

**2. Is there a free way to see my credit reports?**
Yes. AnnualCreditReport.com is the official free site. You can get reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, and they're free weekly.

**3. Would Netflix and Spotify count if I turn on bill reporting?**
Not as far as the app is concerned. Bill Reporting covers only utility, phone and internet bills paid from your linked bank account. Streaming services like Netflix and Spotify aren't included. Those payments are also reported only to Equifax, not Experian or TransUnion. Bill Reporting is free, and your profile shows it isn't turned on yet.

Next step: Check your Equifax report at AnnualCreditReport.com so you can see which accounts are already on file.

cases.message: ok two things. my bank card got hit with a 30 day late back in 2024, it was a one time slip on my part, is there any way to get it taken off before my mortgage app? and if i sign up for the $6 credit builder and pay it like a week late one month, does that show up as a late on my report?

routing.reason: The member asks about removing an accurate 30-day late from 2024 before a mortgage application (goodwill letter or dispute options) and whether a one-week-late Credit Builder payment gets reported as a late, which is covered by payment-history and credit-builder-account.

cases.reply:
**1. Removing the 2024 late payment**

Your profile shows a late payment on your bank credit card, 30 days late, reported December 16, 2024 (first past due November 12, 2024). Accurate late payments can stay on your report for up to 7 years from that first past-due date, and no one can force early removal. Paying a company to remove it is not a legitimate option.

You can still ask. A goodwill letter asks the bank, as a courtesy, to remove the late mark. The bank does not have to agree, but a one-time slip on an otherwise clean account is the situation where it sometimes does. Write a short letter, explain the circumstances, and keep your expectations realistic.

If you think the late mark is wrong (for example, the date or the 30-day status is inaccurate), you can dispute it with the bureau and the bank, with documents. Disputes are only for inaccurate or incomplete information.

**2. Paying the $6 Credit Builder a week late**

A payment 1 to 29 days late is not reported as late. It only gets reported as late once it is 30 or more days past due. So a payment a week late would not show up as a late on your report, though a late fee may apply. Paying before day 30 keeps it from being reported.

Each payment is reported monthly, a few days after it posts, so the plan would add a new monthly record to your report.

Since your mortgage application is in 2027, the goodwill letter is worth sending early, and your on-time rent payments (4 months reported so far) are also building history.

Next step: Draft a short goodwill letter to your bank card issuer about the late reported December 16, 2024, and send it well before your mortgage application.

Also a coworker settled his credit card for way less than he owed. Could your settlement service do that with my card so I pay less than the $550? And last one, can I check if I'd get approved for a Marketplace card without a hard pull?

routing.reason: The member asks three things: why rent is missing from Equifax (rent-reporting), whether the Debt Settlement service can settle their $550 card debt (debt-settlement), and whether they can check approval odds for a Marketplace card without a hard pull (marketplace-offers).

cases.reply:
**1. Why isn't your rent on Equifax?**

Nothing is broken. The app reports rent to TransUnion and Experian only, not Equifax. So your rent won't show on Equifax reports or in scores based on Equifax data. Your profile shows 4 months of on-time rent reported since June 1, 2026, so it should appear on TransUnion and Experian.

Whether rent helps your score depends on two things: the bureau (TransUnion or Experian) and whether the scoring model counts rent. Some models ignore it. Ask your mortgage lender which score and bureaus it uses, because that decides whether rent counts.

**2. Could settlement work on your $550 card balance?**

Your profile shows no debt settlement service on file, and the service only covers accounts that are charged off or in collections. Your bank card is open and current, so it doesn't qualify.

If the service were used on a qualifying account, the fee is 20% of the amount saved, charged only after a settlement is agreed and you make a payment under it. Outcomes vary, and creditors don't have to agree. Settling also doesn't remove the account from your report, and forgiven debt may be taxable, so a tax professional can help you check that.

Your other option is to negotiate directly with the bank for free, or talk to a nonprofit credit counselor.

**3. Can you check if you'd get approved for a Marketplace card without a hard pull?**

Some card issuers offer prequalification, which is usually a soft check that doesn't affect your score. Prequalification is not approval, and I can't tell you your approval odds. The issuer sets the terms and makes the decision. Marketplace partners may pay the app when a user is approved for an offer.

Applying usually triggers a hard inquiry, which can lower your score a little for a short time. Your utilization is 22% ($550 of $2,500), and you have no recent hard inquiries, so a new card isn't urgent. Paying the balance down helps your ratio without any inquiry.

Next step: Ask the bank whether your mortgage lender uses Equifax, TransUnion, or Experian, and which score model they use.

cases.message:
Getting my credit ready for a mortgage in 2027, so a few things:
1) If a landlord ever sent unpaid rent to collections, would paying it off get it off my report?
2) Do my phone and electric bills help my credit the way my rent reporting does?
3) Should I pay my card down to $0 before the lender pulls my credit?

routing.reason: The member asks three questions: whether paying an unpaid rent collection removes it (collections), whether phone and electric bills build credit compared with rent reporting (bill-reporting and rent-reporting), and whether paying the card to $0 before a mortgage pull helps (utilization). Limited to four, most important first.

cases.reply:
**1) Would paying unpaid rent in collections get it off my report?**

Not by itself. Paying a non-medical collection does not remove it from your report. It will show as paid, and it can stay for up to 7 years from the original date you first fell behind. Scoring models like VantageScore 3.0 and 4.0 ignore paid collections, but a lender may use an older model that does not. If you ever face this, you could ask the collector about options, and a legal aid office or attorney can explain any deadlines in your state.

**2) Do my phone and electric bills help my credit like rent reporting does?**

Partly, and in a different way. Your profile shows Bill Reporting is off. If you turn it on, on-time utility, phone, and internet payments from your linked bank account go only to Equifax. Rent reporting goes to TransUnion and Experian. So the two cover different bureaus. Whether either one shows up in a mortgage score depends on which bureaus and scoring model the lender uses.

**3) Should I pay my card down to $0 before the lender pulls my credit?**

You don't need $0. Your profile shows your overall utilization (how much of your card limits you use) at 22%, with $550 on a $2,500 limit. Common guidance is to stay under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better. Issuers usually report your statement balance, so paying down before the statement closing date lowers what gets reported. Paying in full each month is fine. You don't need to carry a balance or pay interest.

**Mortgage timing:** Ask the lender which score model and bureaus it uses. That tells you whether your rent history counts.

Next step: Check your card's statement closing date and pay the balance down a few days before it.

Paying your current phone bill on time doesn't show up on your credit report by itself. Many phone companies don't report on-time payments to the credit bureaus, so that history is often missing. Your profile shows the $1,200 phone collection is unpaid and was first delinquent in March 2022. It can stay on your report until about March 2029. Paying it would show as paid, but it would not remove it. Before you pay or agree to anything in writing on an old debt, check the state deadline for suing, since in some states a payment can restart it. A legal aid office or attorney can check that for you.

cases.reply:
**Disputing the amount**

You can ask the collection agency to prove the debt. Send a written request for validation, which is a letter asking them to show what you owe and how they calculated it. Ask for the original creditor's name, an itemized breakdown showing the $1,200 principal and any fees or interest, and proof they have the right to collect it. Send it in writing (keep a copy and proof of mailing), and do it within the validation period listed in their letter, which is 30 days from when you received it. If you dispute in writing within that window, the collector must stop collecting the disputed amount until it sends verification. The letter you got in late September should show the exact end date, so check it now.

You can also dispute the entry with the credit bureaus if the amount or details on your report look wrong. Attach any records you have. A dispute is for information that is inaccurate or incomplete, so only raise fees you believe were never agreed to or not properly added.

Also, before you make any payment or written promise to pay, check how old this debt is. Your profile shows the original delinquency was March 2022. A payment or written promise can restart the state deadline for lawsuits in some states. A legal aid office or attorney can tell you what applies where you live.

**Keeping your store card on time**

Your store card is open and current, and you paid it on time on October 1. To protect that:

- Set autopay for at least the minimum payment, so a due date can't slip.
- Add a phone reminder a few days before each due date.
- Pay the full balance when you can, so you never carry a surprise amount.

Payments are generally reported as late only once they are 30 or more days past due, but a late fee can still hit sooner, so autopay helps with both.

Next step: Find the validation end date in the September letter from the collection agency and mark it on your calendar.

cases.reply:
**1. Can the bank keep coming after you or sue you while you're negotiating?**

Yes, the bank can still contact you and ask for payment while your debt is in negotiation. Debt Settlement enrollment doesn't stop collection by itself, and the guidance I have doesn't say whether the bank can sue. That depends on your state's rules and the bank's choices. The bank's account is still open on its side, so it's worth knowing that a lawsuit is possible.

If you get a call, letter, or court papers, don't ignore them. Missing a court response deadline can lead to a default judgment against you. If you're served with a lawsuit, contact an attorney or a local legal aid office right away. For questions about your specific rights, a legal aid office or attorney can give you advice. I can't.

**2. Would a missed rent month be reported as late if you're in Rent Reporting?**

No. Late rent is never reported. If a month is missed, that month simply isn't reported. You don't have a Rent Reporting plan on your profile right now, so this applies only if you enroll. If you do, pay your landlord on time as a habit, since a missed month still matters for your relationship with your landlord.

**3. Should you pay the store card to $0 before the statement?**

Your profile shows the Store card at $280 out of an $800 limit, which is 35% utilization (how much of your card limits you're using). That's above the 30% guideline. Your overall utilization is the same 35%, since the store card is your only open revolving account.

Paying the balance down before the statement closes lowers the amount reported to the credit bureaus. Getting to $0 isn't required. Getting under 30% is a good goal, and under 10% tends to be better. At your limit, that means a balance of about $240 or less for 30%, or about $80 or less for 10%. Paying in full each month is good for avoiding interest, but you don't need to carry a balance.

Next step: Before your next statement closes, pay down the Store card to about $80 or less, if you can.

cases.reply:
**1) Will the lender count my rent history?**

Maybe. It depends on the lender. Rent Reporting sends your on-time rent to TransUnion and Experian, not Equifax. cases.message: ok a few things. first, my rent is showing on my TransUnion report but my phone, electric and internet bills aren't, is something broken? second, my score went from 695 to 702 this month, any idea why? and third, I'm moving in the spring, so if the final electric bill slips through the cracks, does it even matter since you only report on-time bills anyway? like if it ended up in collections and I paid it later, would it come off?

routing.reason: The member asks why rent shows on TransUnion but utilities don't (bill-reporting explains Equifax-only utility reporting), why their score rose 7 points this month (score-changes), and whether a bill sent to collections comes off after paying (collections), so these three skills cover all parts.

cases.reply:
**1. Rent shows on TransUnion but bills don't**

Nothing looks broken. Rent reporting and bill reporting go to different bureaus. Your rent reporting sends to TransUnion and Experian. Bill reporting sends only to Equifax, so a TransUnion report will not show your phone, electric, or internet payments. Your bill reporting is active and has been since February 1, 2026. If you want to see those payments, check your Equifax report. A score or report based only on TransUnion or Experian data won't reflect them.

**2. Why your score went from 695 to 702**

Your score rose from 695 on September 15 to 702 now. Your profile shows no new late payments and no negative items, and no hard inquiries in the last 12 months. Your utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) is 12%, which is low. Your on-time payment history is steady: 22 Credit Builder payments, 9 Secured Card payments, and October rent. Lenders report monthly, so the change most likely reflects updated balances and steady on-time payments. I can't tell you which factor made the most difference.

**3. Final electric bill and collections**

Yes, it matters. Bill reporting only sends on-time payments, so a missed final bill won't show up through the app. But if the provider sends it to collections, that can hurt your credit separately.

If it did go to collections and you paid it later, the record would still show as paid, and it would stay on your report for up to 7 years from the original date it went unpaid. Paying doesn't remove a non-medical collection. Some scoring models ignore paid collections, but others, including FICO 8, may still count it. The collection clock doesn't restart when you pay.

To avoid this, pay the final bill on time, and confirm your electric account is closed and the final balance is zero before you move.

Next step: Before your move, ask your electric provider for a final bill and pay it by its due date.

cases.message: Is my credit card utilization too high right now?

cases.reply:
Yes, your utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) is high right now. Your profile shows overall utilization at 47%, with $1,410 owed against $3,000 in limits.

Common guidance is to stay under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better. Your overall ratio is well above the 30% mark.

Your per-card ratios are also worth a look:
- **Bank credit card:** $510 of $1,500, about 34%. Above 30%.
- **Retail store card:** $900 of $1,500, 60%. This is the one that stands out most.

Ways to lower the balances that get reported:
- **Pay before the statement closing date.** Card issuers usually report the balance from the statement, so a payment made before that date lowers what's reported.
- **Pay more than once a month** if you can, so the balance is lower when it's reported.
- **Spread the balance** across cards, so no single card is close to its limit.

Most current scoring models only look at the balances reported now. Once lower balances are reported, usually after the next statement, the effect on utilization should show up. Your overall score also depends on everything else on your report.

Next step: Pay down the retail store card first, and make the payment before its next statement closing date.

cases.reply:

Here is what can help:

- **Your recent record:** Your bank card and auto loan are both current, and your 4 months of on-time rent reporting is also helping your history.

Next step: Write a short goodwill letter to your card issuer, using the account name and the month of the late payment, and ask them to consider removing it.

cases.message: If I pay off my Rewards card today, how many points will my score go up?

routing.reason: The member asks how much their score will rise from paying off a credit card today, which is a question about how card balances affect reported utilization and how quickly that shows up in the score.

cases.reply:
I can't predict a point gain, but I can tell you what should happen.

Your Rewards card has a $1,900 balance on a $2,000 limit, which is 95% of that card's limit. Your overall utilization (how much of your total card limits you're using) is 85%, based on $2,550 of $3,000. The common guidance is to keep utilization under 30%, and under 10% tends to be better.

Paying the Rewards card down lowers the balance that gets reported, and most current scoring models look at the balances reported at the time. Lower reported balances usually help, but the timing and the size of any change depend on the scoring model a lender uses and on the rest of your credit report. Your score is 655 (VantageScore 3.0), down from 668 last month.

Paying today may not show up right away. Issuers usually report the statement balance, so a payment helps most if it's made before the statement closes.

Next step: Check your Rewards card's statement closing date, and make a payment before that date so a lower balance gets reported.

- **Talk to a nonprofit credit counselor.** They can help you build a budget and review your options at no or low cost.
